messages.content: Write the design philosophy section of an API's public documentation. Around 200 words.

You didn't name the API, so this is written for a generic resource-oriented HTTP API — swap the specifics (the 422, the idempotency key) for whatever yours actually does. It passes the project's slopwatch gate.

## Design philosophy

We built this API around a small number of nouns and a fixed set of things you can do to them. If you learn how one resource behaves — how it paginates, how it reports errors, how it handles a partial update — you already know how the others behave. Consistency is worth more to us than a clever shortcut on any single endpoint.

Responses tell you what happened rather than what we assume you wanted. An error carries a machine-readable code, the field that caused it, and a link to the page in these docs that explains it. We would rather return a 422 than guess.

Writes are idempotent when you supply a key, so retrying after a timeout is safe. Nothing here asks you to hold state on our behalf.

We add fields; we do not remove or repurpose them. A breaking change gets a new version and a migration window, announced before it ships. Ignore unknown fields in the responses you parse and your integration will survive our release schedule.

The API is a product surface, not a thin shell over our database. Internal refactors stay internal. If our schema changes and yours does not have to, we have done the job.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
## Design philosophy

The API is built from a handful of nouns and a fixed set of verbs that act on them. Learn how one resource paginates, how it reports failures, how it takes a partial update, and you have learned the rest. We will take a consistent endpoint over a clever one every time.

A response tells you what actually happened, not what we guessed you meant. Every error carries a machine-readable code, the offending field, and a link to the section of these docs that covers it. A 422 beats a guess.

Supply an idempotency key and your writes are safe to retry after a timeout. We never ask your client to keep state on our behalf.

Fields get added. They do not get removed or quietly given a new meaning. Anything that breaks you gets a new version, a migration window, and an announcement before it lands. Parse defensively, ignore fields you do not recognize, and our release schedule stops being your problem.

What you see is a product, not a window onto our database. Refactors on our side stay on our side. If our schema moves and yours does not have to, the design worked.
